top.line: Stopping takes perspective, for people and agents alike
top.para: The hardest call is when to stop. Good human teams overshoot, debating GUID randomness or hitting every KPI without moving the business, and perspective is what stops them. Agents have it worse, because their range is the feature, and the answer is constraints that carry perspective, not draconian rules.

s0.line: Past diminishing returns, more work is not more value
s0.para: For people, perspective on attackers, business phase, bottlenecks and good enough is what stops them, and much of seniority is that perspective. Agents can go in any direction, so they keep going. The answer is direction, a mandate, memory, narrowing graphs, a named stop, one kind of work per step and frequent shipping.

s1.line: Variability is the feature, so agents never naturally stop
s1.para: A model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction. What is often called hallucination is better named variability, and it is close to creativity in a person. But an entity that can go anywhere has no natural reason to stop anywhere, a problem people share.

s2.line: Seniority's bigger picture is what tells you to stop
s2.para: A friend warned that a CISO stops caring about half of what an AppSec specialist cares about, and it proved true. From the board, strategy and the full set of risks showed that some AppSec urgencies were not the priority. Experience is moving between tactical and strategic, and knowing when to stop.

s3.line: Good security teams ran out of work, then overreached
s3.para: Once champions, threat modelling and CI checks made security engineering practice, the best teams ran out of real work and debated GUID randomness, though a version 4 UUID has 122 random bits. That was a movie plot. The CISO's job became giving permission to take risks, grounded in who the attackers are.

s4.line: Teams hit every KPI; the business did not move
s4.para: Strong engineers work backwards from metrics, and when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. A Wardley map shows each part's phase: exploring makes polish waste, while town planning may justify it. Deciding not to fix or build something belongs to whoever has the context.

s5.line: Art is knowing when to stop; shipping shows enough
s5.para: Recognising good enough and diminishing returns is the same skill, and teams without direction struggle with it. Shipping often and early is the best feedback loop: if nobody uses it or nothing moved, stop and do something else. Observability shows whether work changed anything outside the team.

s6.line: Agents' wider range means they simply keep going
s6.para: A person's expertise limits their range, but an LLM asked to fix one thing will fix twenty, lacking the perspective that nineteen do not matter. Any capable entity without real tasks makes itself busy, as Parkinson observed in 1955. Past fixes were draconian limits, when the real problems were communication and direction.

s7.line: Constraints should carry the bigger picture, not just forbid
s7.para: Dan Ward's FIRE doctrine favours small scope on purpose. The machinery is direction, a mandate, memory holding strategy, graphs narrowing scope, a stop named in advance such as a token budget, one twelve-minute step of one kind of work, a reviewer with agency, and shipping. Each puts perspective where decisions happen.

s8.line: Name the stop first and give the bigger picture
s8.para: Name a time, token budget or good-enough result before starting, write down which phase you are in, and give the agent the objective and threats. Measure the needle, not only the KPI, keep one kind of work per step with review, and permit leaving things undone, recording why.
